title: Even a Superpower Can't Just Order a Sovereign Country to Comply
hook: The U.S. indicted Mexican officials on drug-corruption charges and threatened economic penalties. Mexico's president said no anyway — a case study in the real limits of sovereignty.
key_points: Sovereignty means no outside power, however strong, can simply compel another state to act within its own borders.
The U.S. indicted 10 Mexican officials on drug-corruption charges in 2026, including a sitting governor and political ally of Mexico's president.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum refused to arrest them, demanding what she called 'overwhelming and irrefutable proof' first — despite having extradited 92 accused traffickers previously.
The U.S. escalated with threats of economic penalties, but Mexico has a history of successfully resisting similar pressure, including a comparable 2020 case.
The impasse shows that military and economic leverage can raise the cost of refusal, but doesn't erase a sovereign government's ability to simply decline.
content_html: International relations runs on a basic fact that's easy to forget when one country is far more powerful than another: sovereignty means a state retains authority within its own borders, and no outside power — not even a much stronger one — can simply order it to act.
extra_html: ProPublica's Tim Golden reports on a stark test of that principle in 2026: the U.S. indicted 10 Mexican officials on drug-corruption charges, including Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, a political ally of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum. Sheinbaum flatly refused to arrest them, insisting on "overwhelming and irrefutable proof" before acting — even though Mexico had previously extradited 92 accused traffickers to the U.S. The Trump administration escalated with threats of economic penalties and warnings from the DEA that the indictments were "just the start," but Mexican officials pointed to a history of successfully resisting comparable pressure, including a similar standoff in 2020. The impasse is a clean illustration of how hard power actually works between sovereign states: military and economic leverage can raise the price of refusal, but it doesn't dissolve a government's underlying ability to simply say no. (This card describes a specific U.S.-Mexico dispute; the general sovereignty principle applies between any two states.)

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

related.title: Soft Power & Hard Power
related.hook: States get their way two ways: by force and money, or by attraction. Knowing the difference between hard power and soft power explains a lot about how influence really works.

related.title: Treaties & International Law
related.hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'sovereignty' mean in the U.S.-Mexico standoff over drug-corruption indictments?
flashcards.back_html: That Mexico, as a sovereign state, cannot simply be ordered by the U.S. to arrest its own officials — it retains the authority to refuse within its own borders.

flashcards.prompt: Why did Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum refuse to arrest the 10 officials indicted by the U.S.?

choices.text: She said the U.S. hadn't provided 'overwhelming and irrefutable proof'
Mexico has no legal authority to arrest its own officials
The U.S. never actually asked Mexico to act

flashcards.explanation_html: Sheinbaum set a high evidentiary bar as her stated reason, despite Mexico's history of extraditing dozens of other accused traffickers.

flashcards.prompt: What does this impasse suggest about hard power like economic threats?

choices.text: It can raise the cost of saying no, but doesn't guarantee compliance from a sovereign government
It always forces immediate compliance from any country
It has no effect on another sovereign state's decisions

flashcards.explanation_html: Mexico's history of resisting similar U.S. pressure — including a comparable 2020 case — shows leverage can fail to produce compliance even when it's real.
